articles.title: In 1926, John D. Rockefeller Jr. backed a plan to restore Virginia's colonial capital; 100 years later, Colonial Williamsburg is unveiling a $600 million five-year expansion and a $10 million gift for civics education
articles.summary: A century ago, a wealthy philanthropist agreed to help save a fading American town whose colonial-era character was disappearing behind petrol stations,
articles.body: A century ago, a wealthy philanthropist agreed to help save a fading American town whose colonial-era character was disappearing behind petrol stations, garages and modern buildings. What began as an ambitious preservation idea backed by John D. Rockefeller Jr. eventually transformed Williamsburg, Virginia, into one of America's best-known living history museums. Now, 100 years after the restoration project began, Colonial Williamsburg is preparing for another major transformation: a five-year investment plan backed by $600 million in fundraising, alongside a $10 million gift to promote education about the US Constitution and civic responsibility, according to the announcement reported by The Washington Post, as the institution marked its centenary.The story began with Reverend Dr W.A.R. Goodwin, rector of Bruton Parish Church in Williamsburg. He had long wanted to restore the town's historic character and preserve its surviving 18th-century buildings. However, turning the idea into reality required financial backing on a scale that was beyond the reach of a local church rector. Goodwin approached several wealthy potential supporters, including industrialist Henry Ford, but did not succeed in securing his backing. His efforts eventually brought him to Rockefeller, the philanthropist and son of Standard Oil founder John D. Rockefeller. The two had first met in 1924, when Goodwin was raising funds for a memorial hall at the College of William & Mary.Rockefeller visited Williamsburg with his family in March 1926. During a later visit in November, Goodwin explained his vision of restoring the former colonial capital. Rockefeller agreed initially to finance architectural sketches before becoming more deeply involved in the proposal. On December 7, 1926, he authorised Goodwin to purchase the Ludwell-Paradise House, the first property acquired for the restoration project.What followed was a much larger effort to recover the town's colonial appearance. Buildings were purchased, restored or reconstructed, while structures from later periods were removed. Architects, archaeologists, historians and craftspeople worked to recreate the Virginia capital as it appeared during the 18th century, when figures such as George Washington and Thomas Jefferson were involved in debates over Britain's rule and American independence.The project gradually developed into Colonial Williamsburg, which opened its historic attractions to visitors as restoration work progressed. The Rockefeller family remained its principal financial backer for five decades. According to the foundation's centenary history, the initial preservation effort eventually grew into a full-scale restoration of the former colonial capital.A hundred years later, the institution is looking beyond the physical restoration of buildings. Its new five-year investment plan will expand the historical periods represented at the site and strengthen its educational programmes. The foundation has raised $600 million through its Power of Place centennial campaign, supported by approximately 180,000 individual donors. The fundraising target was reached eight months ahead of schedule, according to local broadcaster WHRO.The plan will broaden the museum's living-history interpretation beyond the period leading up to the American Revolution. Visitors will increasingly encounter the events and debates that followed independence, including the drafting and ratification of the US Constitution and the adoption of the Bill of Rights in 1791.The expansion will also include reconstructed period buildings, changes to the historic landscape and greater investment in interpreters who bring historical figures and everyday life to visitors. Traditional craftspeople, including blacksmiths and furniture makers, will receive additional support. Educational programmes will also cover archaeology, food, horticulture and historic trades, allowing visitors to explore how people lived and worked in the colonial period.A major part of the new initiative is the National Institute for the Constitution and Civic Virtue. Constitutional scholar Jeffrey Rosen, a professor at George Washington University, will serve as its founding director. The institute is intended to bring scholars with different perspectives together for lectures, discussions and public programmes exploring the Constitution and the responsibilities associated with citizenship.The initiative has received a $10 million gift from former federal judge J. Michael Luttig and his wife, Elizabeth. The institute plans to organise lectures in Williamsburg, Washington DC and partner institutions across the country. It will also develop educational resources for schools, including material that can be used by K-12 teachers.The foundation hopes to connect historical interpretation with contemporary questions about democracy, civic participation and the country's founding principles. Its historical interpreters, who portray figures such as Thomas Jefferson and George Wythe, are expected to participate in some of the institute's programmes, bringing historical debates to life for modern audiences.The timing of the announcement is significant. The foundation's centenary falls in the same year as the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence in 1776. Its five-year plan will continue through 2031, when the United States will mark 250 years since the British surrender at Yorktown in 1781, a decisive event in the American Revolutionary War.The institution has also faced challenges in recent years, including declining attendance and financial difficulties. The new investment plan is intended to strengthen its public programmes, visitor experience and long-term financial position while expanding its national educational role.For Rockefeller and Goodwin, the original ambition was to preserve a town whose historic buildings were at risk of disappearing. A century later, Colonial Williamsburg is attempting to preserve something beyond its architecture: the history, debates and civic ideas that shaped the country. Its next chapter will be judged not only by how successfully it restores the past, but also by how effectively it helps future generations understand it.You use AI every day. articles.title: China used 17,000 tonnes of treated red mud in a 4.9-km expressway subgrade trial; field tests measured over 90 MPa resilient modulus and under 1 mm FWD deflection
articles.summary: Discover how China is revolutionizing road construction by utilizing treated red mud, a byproduct of aluminum production, in a successful 4.9 km expressway trial, achieving impressive strength and environmental safety.
articles.body: Making aluminium leaves a messy leftover behind in the form of a wet, alkaline waste called red mud. Engineers in China tested it on a real expressway to see if it works. In a 2022 study published in the journal Coatings, researchers from the Shandong Transportation Research Institute built an expressway subgrade layer using treated red mud and found that most field test points met road requirements.Why red mud is such a headache Aluminium begins as bauxite ore. Through the Bayer process, factories refine this ore to form alumina, leaving behind red mud. According to the research, each tonne of alumina creates about 1.0 to 1.8 tonnes of it. The waste is alkaline and contains trace amounts of chromium and fluoride. Much of it is stored in open-air heaps, which take up land and can harm the surrounding environment. The paper puts China's stockpile at more than 350 million tonnes, with less than 4% of it used. This is an issue all over the world. In 2020, a review by Michigan Technological University titled ‘Red Mud: Fundamentals and New Avenues for Utilization’ places the inventory of red mud at almost 4 billion tonnes worldwide. The review describes red mud as a dangerous waste with pH values ranging from 11 to 13.Turning waste into road material Raw red mud cannot go straight under a road. The study found that it holds a lot of water, is made of very fine particles and disintegrates quickly when soaked. So the team mixed it with a modifier consisting of cement, phosphogypsum and a polymer at an 8% composition. In the laboratory, the treated mix reached a strength of up to 3 MPa after three days. Samples cured for seven and 28 days lost less than 20% of their strength after soaking in water. Treatment also reduced the leaching of toxic substances. Hexavalent chromium dropped by 97.9% and fluoride by 83.4% compared with untreated red mud.Inside the expressway trial The trial section was built in 2015 as part of the Ji-Qing Highway reconstruction and expansion project in China. The treated mix containing 92% red mud and 8% modifier by mass replaced a 0.2 m thick layer of lime-stabilised soil in the upper portion of the roadbed. The trial covered a distance of 4,900 metres or 4.9 km, and the subgrade was 11 metres wide. About 17,000 metric tonnes of red mud were used up, and 14,800 cubic metres of natural soil were saved in the trial. After seven days of curing, the team tested a 200-metre section at 20 points, 20 metres apart in two lanes. At 17 of the 20 points, the resilient modulus, a measure of how well the ground rebounds under load, was greater than 90 MPa. A falling weight deflectometer, which drops a weight on the road and measures how much it sinks, recorded less than 1 mm at 16 of the 20 points. The average strength of core samples was 2.4 MPa. The researchers concluded that the overall bearing capacity was good and satisfied the road requirements.Groundwater, cost, and limits Four wells were laid out on either side of the road to study the effects on groundwater. Eventually, the pH settled between 7.0 and 8.0, while harmful substances stayed below the limits of Class III groundwater. The results are generally similar to those of a conventional road section. They also estimated that treated red mud could save about CNY 10 per ton of compacted earthwork over cement or lime-stabilised soil when the red mud was transported 15 to 20 km. Still, this was one trial, and the bearing tests were performed after only seven days of curing. It isn't a promise for all roads around the world. But it shows how a stubborn waste can have a second life to do a useful job.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1943, Army Airborne serviceman Jim Rudy recorded a voice letter for his wife; 74 years later, their daughter found the forgotten disc and heard his voice again
articles.summary: Laurie Meyer discovers a forgotten voice letter from her father, Jim Rudy, a WWII Army Airborne serviceman, recorded in 1943. This emotional audio captures love, humor, and memories, bridging generations and preserving a precious piece of family history.
articles.body: Some family treasures turn up in very ordinary places. For Laurie Meyer, it was a small vinyl record buried with old family belongings. According to a 41 Action News report from KSHB, she was going through her family heirlooms when she found a recording of her father, Jim Rudy, that he had made during World War II. She had heard it once when she was a little girl, but she couldn't remember what it said. She wasn't sure if the audio could be saved.A message sent before the front lineRudy recorded the message in Chicago on 15 January 1943. At that time, he was in his early 20s and was soon to be sent to the European front lines as part of the Army Airborne. The message was addressed to his wife, June, who was Meyer’s mother. The disc was named ‘Love and Kisses – Jim.’ It later became a long-forgotten family relic. Meyer brought the record to Summit Video Services in Lee’s Summit, Missouri. She was hoping to hear her father's voice on the record. The team transferred the audio from the turntable and cleaned it using digital software. Chad Godfrey, the owner of the store, said that he had seen a World War II record like this just three times in 12 years of running his business. He told Meyer that the audio was perfect.Hearing him again Meyer was anxious to hear the recording. She listened to it with the KSHB team on a Thursday afternoon in March 2017. That was 74 years after it was recorded. The message ran about three minutes long. Rudy began by telling June that it was him remembering her. He hoped the little record would please her because it was different from writing. Meyer had warned that her father had a great sense of humour, and it showed in his words. He told June it would be easy to switch him off if she didn't like it. Yet the message was tender: “I am starving for your love and affection.” Near the end, he joked that his pizza had frozen to his trousers in the cold Chicago January. Then he said he was running out of words and out of record. He signed off by calling her “honey” and promising to write the next night again. For Meyer, it was an unbelievable experience to hear her father's young voice again. Meyer described her father as well-known and much loved. Godfrey called the disc an amazing souvenir and said it was satisfying to bring a piece of the past into the 21st century.A wartime habit Rudy’s record was also part of a wartime habit. The Smithsonian's National Postal Museum explains that the mail options increased in the 1940s to include recorded messages. Servicemen could use phonograph records to record their messages and mail them back home to their families. The American Philatelic Society, which is a non-profit organisation, mentions in an article written by Wayne Youngblood that Pepsi-Cola provided booths for servicemen to send their messages. Families loved these records, the article says, and played them again and again. Godfrey said both Coca-Cola and Pepsi ran promotions with booths like that.It wasn't all history for Meyer. It was about her father in his early 20s, making jokes about frozen pizza and missing his wife. It's a few minutes of fun and love captured just before he left for the front lines. Rudy died in 1990 in Overland Park. But now his young voice is saved, frozen in time forever, and Meyer says future generations of the family will share a part of it.You use AI every day. articles.title: A California school district was ordered by a jury to pay $29 million to a former elementary pupil who alleged years of abuse by a teacher; six related lawsuits involving the same educator are still pending
articles.summary: A school is meant to be a place where children are protected, but a former elementary pupil in California has spent years seeking accountability for abuse
articles.body: A school is meant to be a place where children are protected, but a former elementary pupil in California has spent years seeking accountability for abuse he says he suffered inside a classroom. His civil case against ABC Unified School District has now resulted in a $29 million jury award, making it the first of seven lawsuits involving allegations against the same former teacher to reach trial. The verdict, announced by the plaintiff's lawyers on November 5, has brought renewed attention to claims that the district knew about the educator's alleged misconduct involving other students but failed to act. Six related cases are still pending.The plaintiff, identified in court-related publicity only as J.O., attended Luther Burbank Elementary School in Artesia, California. According to an announcement issued by his legal team at Herman Law, he alleged that he was sexually abused by a teacher when he was a child. The lawsuit accused ABC Unified School District of failing to protect students despite having prior notice of the teacher's alleged sexual misconduct involving other pupils.The case was tried by Herman Law attorneys Greg Glazer and Justin Felton. The jury awarded J.O. $29 million, according to the firm, which announced the result through a November 5 press release. The lawyers said the case was the first of seven involving allegations against the same former teacher to go before a jury. Six other cases have yet to be tried.The allegations raise questions not only about the conduct of the former educator but also about the responsibility of school authorities when concerns about an employee's behaviour emerge. The plaintiff's central argument was that the district had information about alleged misconduct involving other students and did not take adequate steps to prevent further harm. The claims against the district therefore focused on its alleged failure to respond to warnings and protect children under its care.However, the $29 million figure needs an important qualification. A November 9 report by legal publication Daily Journal said ABC Unified had stipulated to negligence and liability shortly before the trial, leaving the jury to determine damages. The publication also reported that the district said it had reached a confidential settlement with J.O. during the trial and, as a result, would not have to pay the jury's $29 million award. The settlement amount and terms have not been made public.The distinction is significant: the jury's award is not necessarily the amount the plaintiff will receive, and the district's account of the settlement should not be confused with the verdict itself. The publicly available announcement from Herman Law did not disclose the settlement. The district's reported position adds a separate development to the case, while the financial terms remain undisclosed.The six remaining lawsuits could now bring further scrutiny to the district's handling of complaints involving the same former teacher. Each case will have to be considered on its own evidence, including the individual plaintiff's allegations and what school officials knew or should have known at the relevant time. The first trial, however, has placed the broader allegations in the spotlight.The teacher has not been publicly identified in the announcement issued by Herman Law. Nor does the release specify the years during which the alleged abuse took place, the plaintiff's age at the time or the precise circumstances in which the district is said to have received earlier warnings.The case comes amid wider scrutiny of how California school districts have dealt with historical claims of sexual abuse. A December 2025 investigation by the Los Angeles Times found that public school districts across the state had faced more than 1,000 lawsuits since 2020 involving allegations of childhood sexual abuse. The investigation also examined how some districts had resolved claims through confidential settlements, raising questions about transparency and public accountability.The newspaper reported that more than 330 cases had been settled for roughly $700 million at the time of its investigation, while the state projected that local education agencies could ultimately face payouts of between $2 billion and $3 billion as cases moved through the courts. The figures reflect a much wider set of claims across California and are not specific to ABC Unified.For school districts, cases of this nature can involve difficult questions about institutional responsibility: whether complaints were received, how they were investigated, whether employees were allowed to continue working with children and whether appropriate safeguards were put in place. In civil litigation, a district's potential liability can depend on what administrators knew or should reasonably have known and whether their response was adequate.The verdict may have concluded the jury's role in the first trial, but it has not brought the wider litigation to an end. With the settlement terms undisclosed and six other cases yet to be heard, questions surrounding the former teacher's alleged conduct and the district's response remain before the courts.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2011, two Los Angeles women began building Baby2Baby; 15 years later, it serves 1.5 million children a year and has distributed 850 million essentials, while its gala honouring Demi Moore raised a record $20 million
articles.summary: An initiative that began as a small effort to get diapers and basic necessities to 500 children in Los Angeles has grown into a nationwide operation
articles.body: An initiative that began as a small effort to get diapers and basic necessities to 500 children in Los Angeles has grown into a nationwide operation reaching 1.5 million children every year. Fifteen years after Kelly Sawyer Patricof and Norah Weinstein took over and reshaped the nonprofit Baby2Baby, the organisation says it has distributed 850 million essential items across the US. Its milestone year culminated in a record-breaking gala that raised more than $20 million and honoured actor Demi Moore.The 15th-anniversary celebration was held on November 14 at the Pacific Design Center in West Hollywood, California. The annual fundraiser brought together actors, musicians, philanthropists and supporters, with Moore receiving the organisation’s Giving Tree Award for her advocacy for children and families. Actor Andrew Garfield presented the honour, while singer Cardi B performed during the evening. The event was hosted by Keke Palmer. According to Forbes, the gala raised more than $20 million, marking the highest total in the event’s history. The money will support Baby2Baby’s work providing children and families experiencing poverty with essentials such as diapers, clothing, formula and emergency supplies.Baby2Baby was originally established in Los Angeles in 2006 as a grassroots initiative that collected and distributed gently used items for babies and young children. In 2011, Patricof and Weinstein took over the organisation, incorporated it and changed its mission to focus on providing new essentials to children in need. In an interview with Los Angeles Magazine, the co-CEOs recalled that they had been exploring ways to work together in the nonprofit sector when they began speaking to homeless shelters, children's hospitals and other community organisations. They repeatedly heard that families struggled to afford basic necessities, particularly diapers. The two women saw an opportunity to address a need that was often overlooked.At the time, Baby2Baby was a small volunteer-run operation. Patricof said it supported around 500 children in Los Angeles in 2011 and operated out of a tiny storefront on Pico Boulevard. Today, the organisation reaches approximately 1.5 million children annually across all 50 states and has warehouses across the country. Its workforce has also expanded from the two women and one intern to around 80 full-time employees, according to Los Angeles Magazine.The scale of its distribution reflects how central everyday essentials remain to its work. Over the past 15 years, Baby2Baby says it has provided more than 850 million items, including 400 million diapers. Its services reach families through nearly 1,000 nonprofit organisations and government agencies, including foster care agencies, schools, hospitals, homeless shelters, domestic violence programmes and disaster-relief groups.Diapers have remained one of its biggest priorities. The co-CEOs shared with Forbes that nearly one in two families in the US struggle to afford them. During the Covid-19 pandemic, when some parents were reportedly resorting to newspapers and towels as substitutes, the organisation began manufacturing its own diapers. Patricof told Los Angeles Magazine that this allowed it to produce them at around 80% less than retail prices and distribute more supplies.The organisation has also expanded beyond its original focus on children's everyday needs. Disaster relief has become a major part of its work, with Baby2Baby responding to more than 150 disasters over the past decade, according to the co-CEOs. Its assistance has included supplies for families affected by wildfires, hurricanes and floods. In 2026 alone, the organisation had responded to 30 disasters by the time of the anniversary gala.Another area of focus is maternal health. Baby2Baby's maternal health and newborn supply kits include diapers, wipes, hygiene products, breastfeeding supplies and postpartum care items. The initiative is intended to help mothers and newborns access essentials immediately after childbirth. The organisation told Forbes that the programme was being piloted in 21 states. It has also secured a $9 million investment from New York State to provide kits to 100,000 mothers giving birth on Medicaid across the state. In California, it has introduced a programme intended to provide 400 diapers to every baby born at participating hospitals.Despite the distribution figures and fundraising milestone, the organisation says demand continues to outstrip what it can provide. The co-CEOs said that Baby2Baby received requests for 1.9 billion diapers in 2026 alone, even though it has distributed 400 million over the past 15 years. They also said around 10 million children remain on its waitlist.For Moore, receiving the Giving Tree Award at the anniversary gala brought the focus back to the everyday challenges faced by parents. In her acceptance speech, she spoke about the reassurance of knowing that her children were safe and had what they needed while she built her career. She also highlighted the relief Baby2Baby can offer families who might otherwise have to choose between necessities such as food, rent and diapers.The record gala fundraising total marks a significant moment for Baby2Baby, but its leaders say the need for basic essentials remains far greater than the supplies already distributed.You use AI every day. articles.title: A New York mother challenged the father's primary physical placement of their children despite a finding that he committed domestic violence; on November 13, appeals judges ordered a fresh review, but the arrangement stays for now
articles.summary: A finding of domestic violence does not automatically determine which parent receives primary custody, but courts must explain how such conduct affects
articles.body: A finding of domestic violence does not automatically determine which parent receives primary custody, but courts must explain how such conduct affects children's welfare when making custody decisions. In New York, a mother challenged a Family Court ruling that gave the children's father primary physical placement despite a finding that he had committed domestic violence against her. The dispute reached the state's Appellate Division after she argued that the lower court had failed to properly consider important evidence and the children's best interests.In a November 13, 2026, decision in Matter of Castro v. Hawkins, available on Justia, the New York Supreme Court's Appellate Division, Fourth Department, reversed the lower court's order and sent the case back for further proceedings. The appeals judges found that the Family Court had not adequately explained its factual findings, assessed the parents' credibility or explained how the finding of domestic violence factored into its custody decision. However, the appellate ruling did not immediately change where the children would live. The existing custody and visitation arrangements will remain in effect until the Family Court makes a fresh determination.Father was granted primary physical placementThe case involved Edward Castro, the father, and Ashley Hawkins, the mother, who were involved in a custody proceeding under New York's Family Court Act. Castro had petitioned the Family Court in Steuben County to modify an earlier custody order. Following the proceedings, the court issued an order on August 6, 2025, granting the parents joint legal custody while awarding the father primary physical placement of their children.Hawkins challenged that decision, arguing that the court had not properly evaluated the circumstances before changing the existing custody arrangement. The appeals court noted that the Family Court had failed to make specific credibility determinations or factual findings on disputed matters raised during the custody hearing. Such findings are important because the trial court is in a better position to assess witnesses and determine whether their accounts are reliable.The judges also explained that an established custody arrangement should only be changed when there is a change in circumstances demonstrating a real need for modification in the children's best interests. However, the lower court had not expressly determined whether the father had established the required change in circumstances before considering whether awarding him primary placement would benefit the children.Domestic violence finding was not properly consideredOne of the significant issues involved the Family Court's finding that the father had committed an act of domestic violence against the mother. The appeals judges said that once such a finding had been made, the lower court was required to consider how the domestic violence affected the children's best interests, alongside other relevant circumstances. It also had to explain on the record how that finding influenced its custody decision. The Family Court had not provided the required explanation.Hawkins also argued that the court had improperly penalised her for reporting suspected child abuse under New York's Social Services Law. However, the appeals court said the available record was insufficient to determine whether this had happened because the lower court had not expressly decided whether her reports were false or made in bad faith.The judges also identified another problem with the original decision. The Family Court had relied on information that was not established during the proceedings, including the number of child abuse reports the mother had made against the father during the previous year and an alleged complaint she had filed against him with the FBI. The appeals court said that relying on facts outside the record was an error because judicial decisions must be based on the evidence presented at the hearing.Case sent back for fresh custody reviewThe Appellate Division also found that the Family Court had not sufficiently examined several factors relevant to determining the children's best interests. These include each parent's ability to provide a suitable home, their emotional and financial capacity to care for the children, the stability of previous living arrangements, the children's relationships with their siblings and, where relevant, their own preferences. Because the lower court had not properly evaluated these issues, the appeals judges said they could not independently determine which custody arrangement would best serve the children.On November 13, 2026, the Fourth Department unanimously reversed the August 2025 order on legal grounds and returned the matter to Steuben County Family Court. The lower court must now make specific findings about whether the father had established the required change in circumstances and whether modifying the previous custody arrangement is in the children's best interests. It may hold an additional hearing if necessary.Importantly, the appeals court directed that the existing custody and visitation provisions remain effective while the case is reconsidered. This means the father retains primary physical placement for now, and the mother has not yet secured a change in custody. The decision therefore requires a more complete judicial review rather than an immediate transfer of the children to either parent.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Wisconsin couple wanted to build a backyard fence for their children with special needs, but the HOA refused; years after the $200,000 settlement, they have filed a new lawsuit against 55 neighbours who are yet to pay
articles.summary: Homeowners Lisa and Michael Newman are back in court, this time against the homeowners association in their De Pere subdivision and dozens of neighbours
articles.body: Homeowners Lisa and Michael Newman are back in court, this time against the homeowners association in their De Pere subdivision and dozens of neighbours who never paid their share of an earlier settlement. The couple filed the new suit this autumn, according to NBC 26, nearly two years after their original legal battle over the HOA's refusal to let them build a backyard fence for their five children with special needs. The case now asks whether the association can be held liable for money its members still owe.A dispute over the fenceThe Newmans bought their home in the Nazcr Trac subdivision in 2017, before any of their children had been diagnosed with autism. Their first child received a diagnosis shortly after the move, a second followed in 2018, and a third in 2020. Because of their conditions, all three children were "unable to understand dangerous situations or monitor their own safety" and "require extra supervision to prevent them from running away". All three have wandered away from their parents or caregivers on several occasions. The family's request for a backyard fence grew directly out of those safety concerns, according to the court ruling. A fence would let the children play outside without the constant risk of slipping away.The Newmans sued the Nazcr Trac Homeowners Association after it denied permission to build a fence. The couple wanted a backyard fence for their home in De Pere, Wisconsin, because their children have special needs. Following the HOA's refusal, they took the matter to court. That lawsuit ended with the association agreeing to pay the Newmans $200,000. Under the deal, each homeowner in the subdivision was expected to chip in $1,350.Not every neighbour was ready to payThe settlement was supposed to end the dispute. However, not every neighbour was enthusiastic about paying their share. Sixty-nine homeowners paid their part after the original lawsuit, but many others did not. Some residents said they had never heard of the fence dispute until the settlement was announced, and they felt the decision had been made without them.One homeowner who received a judgment initially refused to pay. He changed his mind only after getting legal advice. Others stayed quiet, and some are now facing the consequences.Some neighbours described the latest development as a sense of déjà vu. "Why is this coming back to us? It's so unfair," one homeowner, who chose to remain anonymous, told the network.A few others wondered why they had to chip in when they had nothing to do with the dispute. "I did nothing wrong. Why should I pay?" another anonymous homeowner asked.The rest still owe the moneyWhether the remaining 55 homeowners have to pay is still a matter of debate, but attorney Victoria Davis Dávila, who represents the Newmans, says they still owe the money. "There's an outstanding judgment. You had the opportunity to pay. You chose not to pay it," attorney Victoria Davis Dávila said.The new lawsuit names the homeowners association along with the homeowners who have not paid. The attorney also warned that if the balance remains unpaid, the association as a whole could be held responsible. That prospect has left people who have already paid feeling stuck in a problem they did not create.One resident who settled his share said the uncertainty had led him to consider moving away from the neighbourhood. He described the situation in a way that many neighbours seemed to share: nobody knows what happens next.Meanwhile, according to the neighbours, the association is looking for legal representation to respond to the new complaint, and its response is due this week. The Newmans want the matter over as much as anyone, their attorney said.For now, though, a fence that was never built still sits at the centre of a neighbourhood that cannot agree on who should pay for it.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mexico, China push cooperation despite tariff tensions ahead of APEC
articles.summary: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on Tuesday told Chinese President Xi Jinping that Mexico wanted to expand cooperation with Beijing, as the two leaders
articles.body: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on Tuesday told Chinese President Xi Jinping that Mexico wanted to expand cooperation with Beijing, as the two leaders met in Shenzhen ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.The meeting comes as trade tensions between the two countries grew, especially after Mexico approved tariffs of up to 50% on more than 1,400 products imported from China and other countries that do not have free trade agreements with Mexico. The duties, which took effect in January, cover sectors including automobiles, auto parts, textiles, footwear and household appliances.China has criticised the measures, while Mexico has defended them as necessary to protect domestic manufacturing. Despite the dispute, Beijing remains a major economic partner for Mexico, accounting for its second-largest source of imports after the United States. Bilateral trade has exceeded $100 billion annually since 2023.Mexico looks to China for waste-to-energy technologyOne of the areas where Mexico is seeking Chinese expertise is waste management, particularly technology that can convert discarded material into energy while reducing dependence on landfills.Mexico is considering a shift towards a waste-to-energy model as part of its efforts to build a circular economy. The approach could help generate cleaner energy, address waste disposal challenges and free up land currently used for dumping.Ahead of the summit, Mexican environment minister Alicia Bárcena visited Chinese facilities specialising in waste utilisation and water treatment to assess whether their technologies could be adapted for use in Mexico.Mexico's environment ministry said the visit was intended to identify alternatives for improving the country's waste management system.Bárcena also visited the Honghu underground wastewater treatment plant in Shenzhen, which can process up to 100,000 tonnes of wastewater a day.The facility has a public park above ground, with the minister making note and stating that Shenzhen offered an example of how polluted waterways and degraded ecosystems could be restored while creating areas for community use.“The Chinese experience demonstrates that it is possible to move beyond landfills and advance toward a circular economy model,” Bárcena said.First China visit as presidentSheinbaum arrived in Shenzhen on Monday for her first visit to China as president. Her bilateral meeting with Xi had been confirmed by the Mexican presidency ahead of the November 18-19 APEC summit.The Mexican leader is also expected to promote her government's Plan Mexico investment strategy during the visit. Her schedule includes meetings with leaders from Canada, Australia and Vietnam.The Shenzhen summit is expected to bring together several major regional and global leaders, including US President Donald Trump and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Asian version of IEA': Japan proposes regional energy body to tackle oil crises amid Iran war
articles.summary: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Tuesday proposed setting up an Asian energy agency modelled on the International Energy Agency (IEA) to help
articles.body: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Tuesday proposed setting up an Asian energy agency modelled on the International Energy Agency (IEA) to help countries in the region respond to oil supply disruptions and energy crises triggered by conflicts such as the Iran war.Takaichi called for the creation of an oil security task force and a Japan-based regional energy body during a meeting on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila, Philippines.“We would like to position this as an Asian version of the IEA,” Takaichi said, AP reported.Established in 1974 in response to a major oil crisis in the early 1970s, the IEA is an independent intergovernmental organisation that provides energy policy recommendations and coordinates emergency oil stockpiles among its member countries.Japan seeks regional oil security task forceJapan would work with the Indonesia-based Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia (ERIA), an energy security research organisation, to lead the proposed task force, Takaichi said at a meeting of the Asia Zero Emissions Community.The initiative would focus on developing rules for emergency oil releases and sharing supplies from national strategic reserves during disruptions.Takaichi also called for greater regional cooperation in building oil stockpiles and establishing a joint reserve system for Southeast Asia. She suggested that unused oil storage tanks in Japan could be made available to hold reserves for the region.Iran war raises energy security concerns across AsiaThe proposal comes amid growing concerns over energy security following the Iran war, which began in late February. Disruptions to oil shipments from the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz, along with soaring oil and gas prices, have pushed several Asian countries to introduce emergency energy conservation measures.Japan, like several other countries in the region, depends heavily on imported oil and gas, making it particularly vulnerable to supply disruptions.The crisis has also accelerated efforts in parts of Asia to reduce dependence on fossil fuels through alternatives such as rooftop solar power and electric vehicles.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bangladesh tensions rise ahead of Hasina's return; bomb blasts near Dhaka airport injure 3
articles.summary: Tensions are mounting in Bangladesh ahead of ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina's planned return next month, with a series of arson attacks and incidents
articles.body: Tensions are mounting in Bangladesh ahead of ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina's planned return next month, with a series of arson attacks and incidents of violence prompting heightened security across the country. Adding to the concerns, two crude bombs exploded near Dhaka's Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on Monday night, injuring three pedestrians, as authorities stepped up measures to prevent possible political unrest.The explosions took place on Monday night, with one bomb detonating near the airport's outer gate and another in the Jasimuddin area, close to the airport and connecting flyovers, the Dhaka Tribune reported on Tuesday, quoting police.Kamrul Islam Talukdar, officer-in-charge of the Airport Police Station, said miscreants had thrown the bombs from a flyover, causing minor injuries to three pedestrians. Security arrangements have since been strengthened.The blasts come amid renewed tensions over Hasina's possible return in December. The former prime minister, who fled to India in August 2024 after a student-led uprising toppled her government, recently sought a new passport and national identity card, signalling preparations for her return.Bangladesh has witnessed several incidents of violence in recent days, including arson attacks targeting trains, buses and banks. Police have blamed Awami League activists and members of affiliated organisations for some of these incidents. The party has been barred from political activities and elections following Hasina's removal from power.Amid fears of further unrest, law enforcement agencies have drawn up special security plans for Dhaka, Gopalganj and other Awami League strongholds, Bengali daily Prothom Alo reported. Additional police personnel will be deployed throughout December, while intelligence surveillance has been stepped up nationwide.Security has been particularly tightened in Gopalganj, Hasina's home district, which has witnessed incidents of arson and vandalism. Around 2,000 police personnel have been deployed there, along with 10 platoons of the Border Guard Bangladesh and Special Response Battalion personnel.Meanwhile, Hasina faces serious legal challenges at home, including a death sentence handed down in absentia by a special tribunal over the deadly crackdown on protesters during the 2024 uprising. She has denied wrongdoing and questioned the legitimacy of the proceedings.Bangladesh has also sought her extradition from India. New Delhi has acknowledged receiving the requests but has not announced a decision.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Blatant and intentional': India slams Turkey over exclusion from UNGA draft consultations
articles.summary: India slammed Turkey at the United Nations for its \"blatant and intentional\" decision to exclude New Delhi and other member states from consultations on a
articles.body: India slammed Turkey at the United Nations for its "blatant and intentional" decision to exclude New Delhi and other member states from consultations on a resolution on cooperation between the UN and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).India voted against the draft resolution, which was adopted by the UN General Assembly with 112 votes in favour, six against and 39 abstentions. Armenia, Cyprus, Greece, Israel and the US also voted against it. Iraq introduced the resolution, while Turkey served as its facilitator.India's deputy permanent representative to the UN Yojna Patel said the OIC's Permanent Observer Mission chose to exclude the Indian delegation and a number of other countries while circulating successive drafts of the resolution.While delivering India's explanation of vote, Patel also called for an investigation into the working methods adopted by the resolution's facilitator."My delegation has voted against this resolution not only because of its substantive aspects, but also for an even more concerning matter regarding the working methods adopted by the facilitator who convened negotiations on the same," Patel said."This is not only shocking but also sets a bad precedent of delegations excluding specific member states to enable their agendas," she added.Patel also said that despite some delegations registering their objections in subsequent rounds, the "facilitators still chose to not include select countries". Other basic procedures, such as acknowledging inputs, were also "blatantly disregarded", indicating that the exclusion was by design rather than by mistake.She said it was "unfortunate that there are member states who publicly profess commitment to multilateralism and completely turn a blind eye to its core guiding principles".Underlining that the UN was founded on the principles of sovereign equality, inclusivity and multilateral cooperation, Patel said differences of position among member states were inherent to multilateral diplomacy and "cannot, in themselves, justify blatant and intentional exclusion from the consultations on matters before the General Assembly"."My delegation strongly objects to such working methods that try to hoodwink excluded delegations into believing that this was just a technical update, which it was not," she said.In a thinly veiled reference to Pakistan, India also voiced regret that the OIC had "once again allowed itself to be systematically misused by one member state to weaponise OIC resolutions and declarations against India through false and baseless allegations".Pakistan is a founding and prominent member of the 57-member OIC.Greece and Cyprus also raised "serious concerns" regarding the conduct of negotiations under Turkiye's facilitation."Throughout the process, the European Union submitted comments and amendments in good faith, which were neither meaningfully addressed nor accompanied by substantial explanations for their rejection. Furthermore, revised drafts were circulated without adequate consultation," Greece's delegate said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A 14-year-old US student collects used coffee grounds from nearly a dozen cafes to grow oyster mushrooms; through her nonprofit, Fungi For Future, she hopes to reduce food waste and help tackle hunger
articles.summary: A 14-year-old eighth-grader in Bloomington, Indiana, is collecting coffee grounds from nearly a dozen local coffee shops and turning them into material
articles.body: A 14-year-old eighth-grader in Bloomington, Indiana, is collecting coffee grounds from nearly a dozen local coffee shops and turning them into material for growing oyster mushrooms. Gloria Chi started her nonprofit, ‘Fungi For Future’, in March, after starting the project. The initiative gives discarded coffee grounds a second life by turning them into a growing medium for mushrooms.Chi has repurposed more than 122 pounds of coffee grounds in her family’s basement, where mushrooms grow in plastic buckets filled with layers of grounds and straw. According to Indiana Public Media, the project has expanded beyond food production to reducing food waste and helping the environment. She plans to donate harvested mushrooms to Hoosier Hills Food Bank and give the remaining mixture to local orchards and composters.How is Gloria Chi collecting coffee grounds to grow mushroomsChi attends Jackson Creek Middle School and has been collecting coffee grounds from nearly a dozen coffee shops in Bloomington. Her partners include Starbucks, Soma Coffee House & Juice Bar, Crumble Coffee and Bakery, The Inkwell Bakery & Cafe, Hopscotch Coffee and the Bloomington Bagel Company. At Crumble Coffee and Bakery, baristas collect the used grounds in a three-gallon bucket behind the counter on Saturdays instead of throwing them away. Chi collects the bucket before the shop closes. The shop uses at least one five-pound bag of espresso beans daily, and often more during Indiana University semesters. Chi began the project in early March and said collecting the grounds has not always gone smoothly.From a science project to mushroom-growing bucketsChi moved to Bloomington from Pennsylvania in July 2025. Before turning to mushrooms, she tried growing tropical fruit trees, but said the cold weather made the project difficult. She said, “It was, like, really hard because, like, it was cold, and for tropical fruit trees, you need to be warm.”“It was sort of like a failed project.”By September, she had shifted her attention to fungi after researching mushroom cultivation online. She first used a mushroom-growing kit to learn the basics. When those mushrooms died, she decided to try growing them herself.Chi ordered mushroom spawn online and began filling buckets with layers of coffee grounds and straw. In her family’s basement, she has 10 five-gallon buckets with holes drilled into their sides. Pink, blue and pearl oyster mushrooms grow through the openings, while white mycelium spreads through the mixture inside.How oyster mushrooms turn coffee grounds into nutrient-rich compostOyster mushrooms survive by breaking down and digesting dead organic matter. As mycelium spreads through the buckets, it breaks down complex compounds in the coffee grounds. Indiana University biology professor Richard Phillips said, “Fungi produce extracellular enzymes.”“These are enzymes that release out into the soil and are involved in decomposition.”As the grounds decompose, nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium become more available for plants to absorb. The leftover mixture of coffee grounds, straw, and mycelium can then be used as compost. Chi plans to donate it to local orchards and composters after harvesting the mushrooms.She referred to mycoremediation, a process she described as mushrooms cleansing toxic material, and said the mixture should make good fertiliser.What does Gloria Chi hope to achieve through ‘Fungi For Future’Chi hoped her mushrooms could become a sustainable food source.She said, “I'm not growing as many mushrooms as I thought I would.”“I was really hoping I could solve hunger with my mushrooms.”The project has also taken on a wider purpose that is reducing food waste and helping the environment. Phillips said similar projects could potentially grow beyond one basement operation if more people became involved.Phillips said, “It sounds like the kind of project that could probably scale up very well, if it's something that a lot of people got interested and involved in.”“That could definitely have an impact on reducing food waste.”Chi has received $1,500 in grants and continues to apply for further financial support. She is working with food resource organisations around Bloomington. She said, “I am looking into some help from the community.”“I hope I can do this forever but I can’t do all this work by myself.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A California man killed his parents after they repaid debts from his fake investment schemes, then took his children to their house to pretend to discover the bodies; he has now received two life sentences
articles.summary: A California man, Mark Andre Tomas Navarrete, has been sentenced to life in prison for murdering his elderly parents after they repaid debts from his fake investment schemes. Discover the shocking details of this tragic case.
articles.body: A California man who killed his elderly parents after they helped repay debts linked to his fraudulent investment schemes has been sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.Mark Andre Tomas Navarrete, 46, received two consecutive life sentences from Sacramento County Superior Court Judge Michael Bowman on Friday. A jury had found him guilty of two counts of first-degree murder on Monday after prosecutors established that he killed his parents for financial gain, Sacramento County District Attorney Office said in Statement.The victims, Augusto Tacsuan Navarrete, 73, and Marjorie Jane Tomas Navarrete, 70, were killed at their home in June 2024. Prosecutors said their son stood to inherit half of their estate.What drove Navarrete to kill his parents?Investigators found that Navarrete had been deceiving friends and relatives through fraudulent investment schemes, promising to return their money with exceptionally high interest rates.The situation became more strained when his parents began repaying family members for debts their son had accumulated. According to the attorney's office, Navarrete grew resentful of his parents and wanted their money for himself.Prosecutors said the killings were motivated by financial gain. The jury also found that Navarrete had committed multiple murders, an allegation that contributed to the sentence imposed by the court.How Navarrete carried out the killingsOn June 28, 2024, Navarrete drove from his home in Elk Grove to his parents' neighbourhood and left his vehicle a few blocks away, according to prosecutors.He put on a mask and gloves before travelling to their house on a kick scooter. He entered through a side gate to avoid being captured by the Ring camera installed at the front entrance.Once inside, he brought his parents into the garage, where he struck both of them on the head with an object before strangling them, prosecutors said.Navarrete then left in his parents' car and parked it a short distance from where he had initially left his own vehicle. He returned to his car on the scooter and drove away.Later that morning, he sent a text message to his parents asking whether they wanted to come over for dinner, despite knowing they were already dead, according to the attorney's office.The case took another turn when Navarrete's sister became concerned after failing to contact their parents. He subsequently went to their home with his children and pretended to discover their bodies, prosecutors said.DNA evidence and surveillance footage helped investigatorsDetectives from the Elk Grove Police Department found the kick scooter used in the journey inside Navarrete's garage. DNA testing also detected his DNA beneath his mother's fingernails, according to prosecutors.Investigators used footage from Flock cameras and other traffic surveillance systems to trace his movements on the day of the killings. The recordings helped establish parts of the route he had taken between his home and his parents' neighbourhood.The investigation also uncovered the financial circumstances surrounding the murders, including the fraudulent investment schemes and his parents' efforts to repay the resulting family debts.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday described the Quad as a “constructive and trusted partnership” and called for concrete goals for its
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday described the Quad as a “constructive and trusted partnership” and called for concrete goals for its next phase of cooperation.Addressing US president Donald Trump, Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese, PM Modi said Manila had a special connection with the grouping, with officials from the four countries first meeting in the city in 2007. The Quad dialogue was revived there a decade later, in 2017.“It gives me immense pleasure to meet you all. Manila and Quad have shared an age-old and special bond,” PM Modi said, adding that the latest meeting in the Philippine capital marked an important milestone for the grouping.He noted that the foreign ministers of the four countries had met five times since January last year, describing this as evidence of their “political will and shared commitment” to the partnership.“For India, the Quad is a constructive and trusted partnership. From maritime security to trusted supply chains, new technologies to disaster response, it has been our endeavour that the Quad provides trusted solutions,” PM Modi said.The prime minister said he was confident the meeting would help set concrete goals for the next phase of cooperation. He also thanked the other leaders for their continued support and personal contributions to the partnership.Trump calls PM Modi a 'tough man', 'great leader'During the meeting, Trump praised PM Modi, describing him as a friend and a leader respected around the world.“He is a tough man. He is my friend. He is a great leader and respected all over the world,” Trump said, adding that Washington and New Delhi had “outstanding relationships” and were coordinating closely.Also check: 'Tough man, great leader': Trump heaps praise on PM Modi at crucial Quad meetingThe Quad meeting was held on the sidelines of the Asean summit in Manila and marked the first leaders-level gathering of the four-nation grouping since September 2024.Quad meets amid shifting regional equationsThe meeting comes as Trump prepares to travel to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit and talks with Chinese president Xi Jinping. The possibility of a meeting with Russian president Vladimir Putin has also been raised.The Quad, comprising India, the US, Japan and Australia, has expanded its agenda beyond traditional security cooperation to include critical minerals, resilient supply chains, emerging technologies, infrastructure and disaster response.Maritime security, commercial shipping routes, access to vital minerals and cooperation in areas such as artificial intelligence and semiconductors are among the key areas of interest for the grouping.Ahead of the meeting, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the Quad was not directed against any particular country, including China.For India, the summit is part of a wider diplomatic engagement with Southeast Asia. articles.title: Sunderland e-motorbike killer's jail sentence increased
articles.summary: Billy Stokoe, then 18, hit Gloria Stephenson, 86, on a zebra crossing in Sunderland, then rode away.
articles.body:
A man who knocked down and killed an 86-year-old grandmother while on an illegal e-motorbike has had his jail term increased by almost two years after the initial sentence was ruled unduly lenient.

Billy Stokoe, then 18, had taken cannabis and was using a mobile phone when he hit Gloria Stephenson on a zebra crossing in Sunderland last year and then rode off, leaving her dying.

In May this year, Stokoe was given a sentence of six years and nine months after admitting causing death by dangerous driving.

That was referred to the Court of Appeal on behalf of Solicitor General Andy Slaughter and the Court of Appeal has now raised it to eight years and six months.

Suki Dhadda, for the Solicitor General, told the court that "whatever sentence is imposed it cannot reflect the loss of a life".

Dhadda said Stokoe, who is now 20, "was performing an obviously highly dangerous manoeuvre" by riding the e-motorbike - which had only one working brake - with one hand.

The barrister said the sentencing judge either used the wrong starting point for the sentence, did not increase the sentence enough because of the aggravating elements of the crime "or gave too much weight to the mitigation", making the sentence unduly lenient.

Dashcam footage showed Stokoe did not slow down or try to avoid Stephenson, who was walking her daughter's dog and trying to complete her 10,000 steps a day.

Stokoe was thrown off the motorbike but did not stop at the scene.

Instead, he rode away to change his clothes and hide the machine at a friend's house before handing himself in at a police station just over an hour later.

He appeared at the appeal hearing via a link from HMP Deerbolt in County Durham.

His barrister, Helen Towers, said Stokoe had been "glued to his phone" as he was riding the motorbike and argued the sentencing judge at Newcastle Crown Court did not make a "gross error".

Lord Justice Stuart-Smith, sitting with Mrs Justice Farbey and Judge Mark Lucraft KC, said there should have been a "significant" uplift to the starting point of the sentence.

Stephenson, who was a mother to four daughters and had 13 grandchildren, had been widowed three times and enjoyed a successful career in the NHS.

She was described by her family as having a "zest for life".

Following the initial sentencing hearing, her eldest daughter, Julie Francis, said she was "absolutely furious and so disappointed" at the sentence given to Stokoe.

"He killed our mam, he left the scene," she said.

"He tried to hide the evidence and he has shown no remorse."

Francis had told the court during sentencing, Stokoe had "left our beautiful, clever courageous mam to die at the side of the road like she was a piece of rubbish in the gutter".

"Our righteous anger is overwhelming," she added.

articles.title: Palestinian woman, 72, shot dead by Israeli settlers in West Bank, health ministry says
articles.summary: Palestinians say there was an attack by settlers in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, while the Israeli military says the settlers fired after being attacked.
articles.body:
A Palestinian woman in her 70s has been shot dead, and several other people wounded, in a village in the occupied West Bank where Israeli settlers recently moved in, the Palestinian health ministry says.

There are conflicting accounts of what happened. Local Palestinians said there was an attack by settlers in part of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, near Jericho, which is meant to be under the full control of the Palestinian Authority.

According to the Israeli army, there was a Palestinian car-ramming attack on an Israeli vehicle. It said rocks were then thrown at the Israelis, who opened fire in response.

There have been high tensions in the area since a group of settlers recently set up a new outpost.

They moved into eight houses in the village on 4 November after buying them, they have said, in a secretive operation. The properties are in an area where Israel retains full security control.

All settlements are illegal under international law.

Palestinian reports said Fadwa al-Fahidat, who was 72, was shot outside her home on Monday evening and that, hearing the news, her son sped to the scene in his car.

He then collided with an empty Israeli vehicle parked outside his family home and settlers standing nearby were injured, they said. The settlers then began shooting, the reports said.

The statement from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that "terrorists accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it", and then "exited their vehicle with weapons and attacked and harmed the occupants of the Israeli vehicle".

Afterwards, it said, "rocks were hurled at the Israelis, who responded by firing in order to remove the threat." It did not mention the fatal shooting of a woman.

The IDF said that Israeli security forces were sent to the scene and were pursuing suspects.

Doctors at a hospital in Jericho said that al-Fahidat was shot in the head. Several other Palestinians and Israelis were injured, reports said.

The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem says there has been a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, with Israeli troops now stationed nearby to secure the new settlement.

Residents and activists say armed settlers walk and drive quad bikes around the neighbourhood as they threaten Palestinian residents.

In a separate incident on Monday evening, eight Palestinians were injured when they were hit by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler on a main road in Tuqu, south of Bethlehem, according to Palestinian officials and the Palestinian Red Crescent.

The IDF said the incident was a traffic accident. But the Palestinian foreign ministry called it a "terrorist attack", saying the driver hit a group of Palestinians who had gathered near the scene of an earlier traffic accident.

Also on Monday, the Civil Administration - the body that implements Israeli government policy in the West Bank - announced the allocation of more than 28 sq km (6,945 acres) of land in the northern Jordan Valley to nine settlers for grazing, according to the Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now.

It said handing over vast tracts of land to settlers for grazing outposts constituted "direct support for the systematic expulsion of Palestinians from their lands and the rampant criminal violence in the West Bank".

It is the first sanctions package since Foreign Secretary David Miliband's pledge in September to respond to the accelerating rate of settlement expansion in the West Bank, which he said risked rendering a two-state solution unviable.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi picked up a small Indian flag being used as a spot marker during a group photograph of Quad leaders in Manila on Tuesday, prompting a reaction from US president Donald TrumpThe moment unfolded as PM Modi was taking his place alongside Trump, Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese and Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi for the media ahead of their meeting on the sidelines of the Asean summit in the Philippine capital.As PM Modi picked up the flag marker, he said he could not leave the national flag on the floor.“I cannot put (leave the flag) on the floor,” he said.Trump responded: “Save it.”The gesture recalled a similar moment during the 2023 BRICS summit in Johannesburg, when Modi picked up an Indian flag marker from the stage.The photograph preceded the Quad leaders' meeting, during which PM Modi described the grouping as a “constructive and trusted partnership” and called for concrete goals to guide its next phase of cooperation across the Indo-Pacific.PM Modi highlights Quad's role in Indo-PacificAddressing the other three leaders, PM Modi pointed to Manila's long association with the grouping. Officials from the four countries first met in the city in 2007, while their dialogue was revived there in 2017.He said the foreign ministers of the four countries had met five times since January last year, calling this evidence of their “political will and shared commitment” to the partnership.“For India, the Quad is a constructive and trusted partnership. From maritime security to trusted supply chains, new technologies to disaster response, it has been our endeavour that the Quad provides trusted solutions,” he said.PM Modi expressed confidence that the meeting would help establish concrete goals for the next phase of cooperation and thanked the other leaders for their continued support.Trump praises PM Modi, announces Quad initiativesTrump also praised PM Modi during the meeting, calling him a friend and a leader respected around the world.“He is a tough man. He is my friend. He is a great leader and respected all over the world,” Trump said, adding that relations between the US and India were “outstanding” and that the two countries were coordinating closely.Trump also outlined four initiatives emerging from the meeting: a Quad Business Leaders' Forum, a Super Intelligence Accelerator, a Maritime Intelligence Sharing Corporation and cooperation on cybersecurity intelligence-sharing.The Quad, comprising India, the US, Japan and Australia, has broadened its agenda beyond traditional security concerns to include resilient supply chains, critical minerals, emerging technologies, infrastructure and disaster response.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
