articles.title: Licensed to subvert: How Robert Pattinson outran Twilight, conquered Gotham, and became James Bond
articles.summary: Just before 8.30 pm (IST) on Monday, November 16, 2026, the official James Bond social media accounts abruptly wiped their feeds clean and typed out a
articles.body: Just before 8.30 pm (IST) on Monday, November 16, 2026, the official James Bond social media accounts abruptly wiped their feeds clean and typed out a repeating two-word transmission: “Identity confirmed”. Moments later came the photograph: Robert Pattinson in a crisp black tuxedo, stepping into cinema’s most scrutinized silhouette.Exactly 20 years after Casino Royale held its London premiere to introduce Daniel Craig, the 40-year-old Londoner was unveiled as the seventh official 007. Even Buckingham Palace chimed in on Instagram: “Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond”.To anyone whose mental snapshot of Pattinson is still frozen in late-2000s pop-culture ridicule—the pale, sparkling vampire of Twilight—the casting looked like a shock. To anyone who has followed his career trajectory over the past 15 years, it looked almost inevitable.Since surviving the global teen-idol frenzy that threatened to trap him, Pattinson has engineered one of Hollywood’s smartest, strangest, and most thrilling second acts. He traded easy studio paychecks for nocturnal indie thrillers, claustrophobic art-house dramas, and daring collaborations with top auteurs, before striding back into mega-franchises entirely on his own terms.Now he faces an unprecedented balancing act. Never in Hollywood history has one actor played both Batman and James Bond at the same time. Juggling Gotham and MI6—while following Craig’s physically battered, emotionally scarred Bond under the direction of Dune filmmaker Denis Villeneuve—is an uphill task. The weight of expectation apart—which has undone many stars—there are practical scheduling problems that will crop up. And then comes the mother of all risks — the creative kind.But if any actor is equipped to manage that gamble, and push 007 somewhere genuinely new, it is the dry-witted, quietly menacing performer who turned Tenet's tailored spycraft into a dress rehearsal and became every major director's dream collaborator.From Barnes Theatre Club to the eye of the Twilight stormPattinson's path to Her—now His—Majesty's Secret Service began with far less calculating motives in Barnes, southwest London, where he was born on May 13, 1986, to a classic-car dealer father and a mother who worked for a modeling agency.As a schoolboy, he wandered into the amateur Barnes Theatre Club. “I wouldn’t be acting if it wasn’t for that little club,” he said in an interview back in 2008 – the beginning of the Twilight saga. “I went originally because a lot of pretty girls went there”. It would just take a few months in 2008 after the first Twilight movie released for him to become the fantasy boyfriend of teenage women around the world.Pattinson started backstage before landing lead parts at Barnes Theatre Club because, “all the good people left and I was the only one tall enough to play the lead”. That self-deprecating humour, and the slick opportunist in him would make him the superstar—on his way to become a megastar—of today. This does not happen without fierce ambition, a bit of luck, and a canny sense of career longevity. Like moving from mainstream to arthouse to indie to mainstream back again with an ease that won over audiences, critics, studios and directors alike.So, Pattinson’s journey began like this. His scenes were cut entirely from Mira Nair's Vanity Fair, and then he landed his first major break—cast at 17 and debuting on screen at 19—as the ill-fated Hogwarts champion Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (2005), produced by David Heyman – the very man now co-producing his Bond debut.Back then, he was an intense loner – far from radiating the present 007 swagger. “Right at the beginning, I literally just sat by myself and never talked to anyone,” he recalled on the film’s DVD extras. “I just drank like 25 cups of coffee every day”.Three years later, at 21, he arrived at an audition for Twilight (2008)—only his fourth film—having taken a Valium for the first time in his life. “I just remember feeling so glorious in the back of the taxi with the window open,” he told GQ in 2022. “I think I had this quite spacey, detached kind of thing in the audition, which must have worked for the character”.Across five films that grossed more than $3.3 billion worldwide, Edward Cullen turned Pattinson and co-star Kristen Stewart into global obsession targets, with their real-life four-year relationship dissected everywhere from supermarket tabloids to Donald Trump’s social media feed (Google this).Fame at that pitch brought expected results — mockery alongside mania. Skeptics sneered at the glossy teen-vampire melodrama, even as veteran film journalist Steven Gaydos foresaw something others hadn’t. Pattinson and Stewart’s “mutual star power obscured the franchise's loopy werewolves-and-vampires silliness and kept the focus on love and heat between two major new charismatic movie stars”.For Pattinson, the glare felt suffocating. “Nothing, I don’t think, can prepare you for the fans,” he admitted during the Twilight fever. “I’m completely overwhelmed every time”. In 2011, he described the pressure of living inside a public projection: “When the whole world is watching you, they create stories and give you labels that have nothing to do with you. It’s almost impossible for you not to explode!”What saved him from becoming a punchline though was that he reached for the needle before anyone else could. Long before the Twilight saga ended, Pattinson began puncturing his own heartthrob image with dry, self-deprecating British humour. Reading the Twilight material, he told The Guardian in 2011, he thought Edward was “the most ridiculous person who’s so amazing at everything... And the more I read the script, the more I hated this guy, so that’s how I played him – as a manic-depressive who hates himself. Plus, he’s a 108-year-old virgin, so there’s clearly some issues there”.On press tours, he weaponized deadpan absurdity—attributing his wilder remarks to “a little gremlin inside of me that thinks, ‘Just say something shocking. You're only here for a few minutes, say something terrible’”. Whether claiming he saw no point in washing his hair or fabricating tall tales like witnessing a clown die in an explosion, he kept interviewers off-balance.Beneath the jokes, though, sat a genuine dread of stagnation. “If I do decide one day to stop acting,” he told The Guardian, “I just hate the idea of people going: ‘Oh, did you ever do anything else besides that Twilight thing?’”The auteur apprenticeshipMost young actors handed a $3.3 billion launchpad spend the next decade playing it safe with glossy studio romances or formulaic action. Pattinson used his Twilight fortune—noting that financial freedom “keeps the door open to make what you want to make”—to disappear into the arthouse.In hindsight, it looks like a brilliant masterplan, yet at the time he was wracked by insecurity. Asked during the 2012 release of David Cronenberg’s Cosmopolis whether he felt sure he was even an actor, he replied simply: “No”. “As soon as you start existing in a certain world, you feel like you have a tremendous amount of baggage all the time,” he explained. “You get stuck in this rut where you want people to think you’re something else, but you’re too scared to do what that is to actually be the other person”.Even through that self-doubt, he kept picking projects designed to burn off his teen-idol baggage. In Cosmopolis—which The Guardian critic Peter Bradshaw retrospectively calls his most intriguing “pre-Bond or proto-Bond outing”—Pattinson played an alienated billionaire gliding across Manhattan in a stretch limo, cultivating a “tough, invulnerable carapace”.He worked with Werner Herzog (Queen of the Desert), then vanished behind a moustache and understated poise as an Amazon explorer’s loyal second-in-command in James Gray’s The Lost City of Z (2016).The decisive turning point came in 2017 with Benny and Josh Safdie’s nocturnal thriller Good Time. As Connie Nikas, a desperate, volatile small-time New York criminal careening through one catastrophic night to spring his brother from custody, Pattinson proved he belonged among the fiercest screen actors of his generation.He followed it with Claire Denis's unsettling sci-fi drama High Life (2018) and Robert Eggers’s The Lighthouse (2019), where he spent weeks bickering, drinking, hallucinating, and unraveling alongside Willem Dafoe as a 19th-century lighthouse keeper. “Whenever you find something where you don’t really have any kind of archetype to fit it into, you don’t have any crutch of something you’ve done before, it’s always so exciting,” he said while promoting The Lighthouse. His guiding rule was blunt: “Nothing can be good if you do it for money or for fame”.Why auteurs and studios chase PattinsonIf the 2010s won back his artistic credibility, the 2020s turned Pattinson into an industry unicorn—an actor equally coveted for big-budget tentpoles and radical character pieces. That synthesis clicked into place in Christopher Nolan’s Tenet (2020), where Pattinson stole scenes even from the lead actor, as Neil, an effortlessly sharp, slightly seedy British intelligence operative who moved through global espionage intrigue in custom-tailored suits. Foreshadowing?Off-screen, his curiosity left its own mark on cinema history: near the end of Tenet's production in 2019, Pattinson gifted Nolan a book of J. Robert Oppenheimer’s speeches, a present that sparked Nolan’s decision to make Oppenheimer (2023).Two years later, Matt Reeves’s The Batman (2022) quieted the remaining doubters. Stripping Bruce Wayne of traditional playboy glamour, Pattinson portrayed a brooding, rage-prone loner—played with what The Guardian called “appealing vulnerability,” yet possessing “eccentricities to the point of being psychopathic,” as another critic put it.Even while donning the cape and cowl, he couldn’t resist mocking superhero vanity, telling GQ during lockdown that he had stopped working out (“I think if you're working out all the time, you’re part of the problem”) before admitting he simply found bragging about gym routines embarrassing.His 2025–2026 run has only widened the gap between him and his peers. He played multiple versions of an endlessly dying space worker in Bong Joon Ho's sci-fi satire Mickey 17 (2025), starred in and executive produced Lynne Ramsay's marital crisis drama Die, My Love opposite Jennifer Lawrence, anchored Kristoffer Borgli's dark wedding satire The Drama (2026) alongside Zendaya, turned ruthless as the suitor Antinous in Nolan's The Odyssey (2026), and chilled Venice Film Festival audiences as To Catch a Predator presenter Chris Hansen in Lance Oppenheim's Primetime (2026).Next month, in December 2026, he appears as the shapeshifting conspirator Scytale in Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three, before Fernando Meirelles’s The Take arrives in 2027.Directors keep returning to Pattison. Possibly because he brings more than technical skill to a set. “Part of the reason Rob is one of the great actors of our time is his taste,” Oppenheim said. “He’s incredibly well-read and watches a ton of movies. He thinks like a filmmaker”. Villeneuve—with whom Pattinson has said working is “never really a stress”—declared in an official statement that Pattinson “has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new”.Producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman praised “his fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit, and his ability to continually reinvent himself,” while Amazon MGM Studios film chief Mike Hopkins pointed to his “remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity”.Gotham meets MI6!Casting Pattinson as Bond breaks more than 60 years of franchise orthodoxy. Under Eon Productions stewards Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, the long-standing rule was that James Bond had to remain a bigger star than any actor playing him, and performers tied to another major screen icon were sidelined. That policy reportedly wasn’t in favour of Pattinson being thought of as an option for Bond though he was thought of as a contender.But the whole playbook changed in early 2025, when Amazon—which acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022—struck a deal reported at more than $1 billion to take full creative control of 007 from Broccoli and Wilson. Under casting director Nina Gold, a search launched in May 2026 tested British contenders including Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, and Nicholas Hoult in London. Yet in a fragile theatrical market where no franchise is bulletproof any more, Amazon MGM pivoted toward an undeniable movie star capable of uniting prestige credibility with Gen Z box-office reach.According to reports, Pattinson’s Bond deal reportedly covers three films rather than the four asked of O’Connor and Lowden — with The Hollywood Reporter cited as saying that Villeneuve personally called Pattinson on Sunday morning to give him the part.That decision places Pattinson on a tightrope no Hollywood actor has ever walked: headlining Batman and James Bond concurrently. The Batman Part II began shooting in London in June 2026 with a cast featuring Scarlett Johansson, Sebastian Stan, Colin Farrell, and Andy Serkis, before pausing in October when Matt Reeves stepped away for a family matter.Steven Soderbergh stepped in to help finish principal photography, and Serkis said that filming has been extended past Christmas into early 2027. So, with The Batman Part II scheduled for February 18, 2028, and Bond 26 eyeing 2027 production for a 2028 release, Pattinson could anchor cinema’s two most iconic solo heroes in the very same year!His original three-film Batman contract reportedly lapsed amid delays, also fuelling speculation that Part II could close his Gotham chapter if 007 dominates his schedule—even though Pattinson recently insisted he wants to play Batman “as long as he can”.Still, as a creative proposition, Pattinson is uniquely built to keep the two icons separate, and elevate the stakes of both. His Batman is a gothic, emotionally stunted recluse lurking in the shadows; his Bond promises outward polish, razor-sharp tailoring, and coiled sociability. An actor who moved convincingly between a mad 19th-century lighthouse keeper, a repeatedly regenerated expendable worker, and a cunning Homeric aristocrat in the span of seven years is unlikely to let Bruce Wayne bleed into 007.The tuxedo, the quiet menace, and the Bond for our timesDaniel Craig closed his five-film, fifteen-year run with the unthinkable: killing James Bond at the end of No Time to Die (2021), the first screen death in the character’s 64-year movie history. Craig's 007 was hard-edged, emotionally scarred, and physically punishing. Attempting to cast a younger copy of that bruiser energy would have trapped his successor in Craig’ s shadow.Pattinson resets the silhouette entirely by reverting to a sharper, subtler British aura. In The Guardian, Peter Bradshaw praised Pattinson’s taller, “more willowy frame” from which a tuxedo hangs with “elegant abandon” – urging the studio not to force him into a five-hour daily gym regimen.Viewers of Tenet already saw how naturally he wears Savile Row polish: gliding through scenes with dry, observant humour and an understated sense that he is always three steps ahead. Bradshaw predicts a Bond armed with a “crinkly-eyed reptilian grin” and a gift for “cool, sensual menace” – one who evokes an Ian Fleming naval officer rather than a musclebound mercenary.Just as important is how Pattinson's sensibility fits the present moment. Film writer Jake Coyle said Pattinson has spent two decades subverting traditional, swaggering masculinity—and arrives as “the funniest and quickest to laugh actor to take on James Bond in decades”.Combined with a 40-year-old’s lived-in maturity, that dry wit can disarm 007’s dated swagger without turning the spy into a wink-filled cartoon. Place that performance inside Denis Villeneuve's frame, working from a script by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight, and the chemistry grows even sharper.Pairing two artists who routinely bend giant franchises to their own instincts guarantees Bond 26 (title of the first film that will star Pattison) will stay massive as well as unique.Two decades ago, a shy teenager sat alone on the Harry Potter set, knocking back 25 cups of coffee a day and wondering if he belonged in the business. Every risk he took after Twilight stripped away the baggage of fame and honed his craft. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team,” Pattinson said in his official statement about inheriting 007.Hollywood’s great shape-shifter has spent 20 years proving no single role can contain him. Now, slipping into James Bond’s tuxedo while Gotham’s shadows still linger at his back, he is ready to pull off the trick of a lifetime.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Admin orders ban on laser lights, meat shops near airport to prevent bird hits
articles.summary: Patna administration bans laser/high-intensity lights and open meat/fish shops near airport, orders waste removal and stray dog control to cut bird-hit risk.
articles.body: Patna: Strict restrictions on laser lights, high-intensity lighting and open meat and fish shops around Jayprakash Narayan International Airport have been ordered to minimise the risk of bird-hit incidents and ensure safe, uninterrupted flight operations. Authorities have also been directed to remove garbage dumping points, improve sanitation and take measures to control stray dogs in areas surrounding the airport.The directions were issued by divisional commissioner Rajesh Kumar during a meeting of the airport environment management committee on Tuesday. He reviewed the steps being taken by various departments to address environmental and safety concerns within a 10-km radius of the airport and directed officials to ensure time-bound implementation of all pending instructions.The administration has asked officials to strictly enforce the ban on laser lights and high-intensity lights at marriage halls and other event venues near the airport.
